header.title: Fasti: AI translation (Claude)
header.author: Ovid
header.source: Translated by Claude (claude-opus-5-5, Anthropic) from the library's phi0959.phi007.perseus-lat2, from the Perseus Digital Library (CC BY-SA 4.0), one English line for each line of the original. Only some passages are translated so far: those that the Atlas of Ancient Myth, Magic in the Ancient Texts and the demons-and-angels study cite.
header.statement: An AI-generated translation. No specialist has reviewed it.
header.availability: CC BY-SA 4.0, as its source requires: credit the Perseus Digital Library and this AI translation, and share adaptations under the same licence.

notes.3.283: 3.339–342: the exchange is wordplay (caput 'head', of an onion or a man; anima 'life', of a man or a fish) that English only partly keeps. 3.341: the text runs 'hominis:sumes' together; read as Jupiter's 'A man's' and Numa's reply.
notes.2.379: 2.400–401: the line break seems displaced; the words 'he would bring help' (ferret opem) belong at the end of 2.400, which is left short. Translated as the lines stand.
notes.5.427: 5.433: the hand-gesture described is unclear. 5.471: 'aequatis' gives no sense and is probably a corruption of 'aequalis' (equal); translated so.
notes.4.807: 4.838, 4.848: the edition prints the enclitic 'que' as a separate word ('sint, que Celer', 'sic que'); read as running text.
notes.2.665: 2.665: 'lectus' is taken as 'read' (his name written on the heaped-up trophy); it can also mean 'chosen'.
notes.1.465: Misprints read as corrected: 'Hesperiarnque' (1.498) for Hesperiamque, 'Angustos' (1.531) for Augustos, and the word division 'di que ... salve te' (1.509) for dique ... salvete.
notes.4.245: 4.263: 'divum que' is read as divumque. The source's quotation marks are irregular here (a stray one at 4.261, none at 4.264 and 4.271); speech is marked by sense.
notes.2.265: Stray footnote numerals in 'Cyllene1' (2.276) and 'obit.1' (2.282) are ignored; 'Lati as' (2.270) is read as Latias.
notes.4.33: 4.45: 'recidiva vocabula Troiae', literally 'revived names of Troy', is compressed; taken as a Trojan name given again.
notes.6.255: 6.268: 'significant sedem terra focusque suam' is compressed; the point seems to be that earth and hearth each stand fixed in their own place.
notes.3.665: 3.670: 'Angebat' is evidently a corruption of fingebat, 'shaped'; translated so.
notes.5.193: 5.194: 'emat' is evidently a corruption of efflat, 'breathes out'; translated so.
notes.5.133: The surname is Praestites, which Ovid derives from praestant, 'they keep [safe]'.
notes.6.295: The name Vesta is derived here from vi stando, 'standing by force'; the Greek name, Hestia, is not given in the text.

nodes.text: Hail, glad day, and always come back better,
worthy to be honoured by a people that rules the world.
But what god am I to say you are, two-formed Janus?
For Greece has no divinity equal to you.
Tell me too the reason why, alone of the heavenly ones,
you see both what is behind and what is in front.
While I was turning these things over in my mind, tablets in hand,
the house seemed brighter than it had been before.
Then holy Janus, wondrous in his two-headed image,
suddenly presented his two faces to my eyes.
I was terrified, and felt my hair stand stiff with fear,
and my breast was cold with a sudden chill.
He, holding a staff in his right hand and a key in his left,
uttered these sounds to me from his front mouth:
‘Put aside your fear and learn, hard-working poet of the days,
what you ask, and take my words into your mind.
The ancients called me Chaos (for I am a thing of long ago):
see of how long a time are the deeds I shall sing.
This clear air and the three bodies that remain,
fire, water and earth, were a single heap.
Once this mass, through the strife of its elements, broke apart
and, dissolved, went off into new homes,
flame sought the heights, the nearer place took the air,
earth and sea settled on the middle ground.
Then I, who had been a ball and a shapeless bulk,
went back into a face and limbs worthy of a god.
Even now, a small mark of my once confused shape,
my front and my back look the same.
Hear what the other reason is for the shape you asked about,
so that you may know it and my duty together.
Whatever you see anywhere, sky, sea, clouds, lands,
all are closed and opened by my hand.
With me alone lies the guarding of the vast world,
and the whole right of turning the hinge is mine.
When I have chosen to send Peace out from her quiet dwelling,
she walks freely along unbroken roads:
the whole world will be mingled with deadly blood
unless rigid bolts keep wars shut in.
I preside over the gates of heaven with the gentle Hours:
Jupiter himself goes out and returns by my office.
Hence I am called Janus; and when the priest sets before me
the cake of Ceres and spelt mixed with salt,
you will laugh at the names: for now Patulcius, and the same god
now Clusius, I am called by the sacrificing mouth.
No doubt that rude antiquity wanted, by an alternating
name, to signify my different functions.
My power has been told. Now learn the reason for my shape:
yet you yourself already see it in some part.
Every door has two fronts, one this side and one that,
of which this one faces the people, and that one the household god;
and just as your doorkeeper, sitting near the threshold of the house front,
sees the goings-out and the comings-in,
so I, doorkeeper of the heavenly court, look out on
the eastern and the western regions at once.
You see the faces of Hecate turning in three directions,
so that she may guard the crossroads split into three ways;
and I, so as not to lose time by turning my neck,
may see two ways without moving my body.’
He had spoken, and with his look had made it plain that, if I wished to ask more,
he would not be difficult with me.
‘You could recognise me under the double image,’ he said,
‘if long time itself had not worn the work thin.
The reason for the ship remains: by ship to the Tuscan river came
the sickle-bearing god, after wandering over the world.
I remember Saturn being received in this land:
he had been driven from the heavenly kingdoms by Jupiter.
From then on the name Saturnia long remained to the people;
the land too was called Latium, from the god's lying hidden [there].
But a good posterity shaped a ship on the bronze,
bearing witness to the arrival of the guest god.
I myself lived on the ground whose left side
the gentlest wave of the sandy Tiber grazes.
Here, where Rome now is, an uncut forest grew green,
and so great a place was pasture for a few cattle.
My citadel was the hill which the common people by our name
call, and which this age calls the Janiculum.
I reigned then, when the earth could bear gods,
and divinities mingled in human places.
here, where you have a temple joined to the two forums?”
He, stroking with his hand the beard that hung down to his chest,
at once told of the war of Oebalian Tatius,
and how the fickle guard, won over by bracelets, led the Sabines
in silence along the path to the top of the citadel.
“From there,” he said, “as it is now, the slope by which you go down
was steep into the valleys and forums.
And already they had reached the gate from which Saturnia,
in her spite, had removed the bars set against them,
when, afraid to join battle with so great a deity,
I cunningly set in motion the work of my own craft,
and by the power in which I am strong I opened the mouths of springs
and shot forth sudden waters;
but first I put sulphur beneath the wet channels,
so that the boiling water would close the way to Tatius.
When its usefulness had been felt and the Sabines driven back,
the place, made safe, was given back the form it had had.
An altar was set up to me, joined to a small shrine:
it burns spelt with sacrificial cakes in its flames.”
Where shall I look for the causes and the custom of these rites?
Who will steer my sails in the middle of the sea?
Advise me yourself, you whose name is drawn from song,
and favour my undertaking, so that your honour does not go astray.
Born before the moon (if it is believed about itself),
the land takes its name from great Arcas.
Here lived Evander, who, though distinguished through both his parents,
was nobler by the blood of his holy mother;
she, as soon as she had taken the heavenly fire into her mind,
would utter true songs from a mouth full of the god.
She had told her son that upheavals threatened him and herself,
and much else besides, which time has proved true.
For the young man, driven out with his all-too-truthful mother,
leaves Arcadia and his Parrhasian home;
as he wept, his mother said to him: “This fortune, like a man
(stop your tears, I beg you), you must bear.
So it was fated; it was not your own fault that drove you out,
but a god: an offended god has driven you from your city.
You suffer not the penalty of guilt but the anger of a deity:
it is something, in great misfortunes, to be free of crime.
As each person's mind is conscious of its own deeds, so it conceives within
the breast hope or fear in keeping with what it has done.
Yet do not grieve as though you were the first to suffer such ills:
that storm has overwhelmed mighty men.
He who was once driven from the Tyrian shores suffered the same:
Cadmus, who stopped as an exile on Aonian soil;
Tydeus suffered the same, and the same Pagasaean Jason,
and others whom it would take too long to tell.
To the brave every land is a homeland, as the sea is to fish,
as to a bird whatever lies open in the empty world.
Nor does the fierce storm rage all the year round:
for you too (believe me) a time of spring will come.”
Evander, his mind strengthened by his mother's words,
cuts the waves in his ship and reaches Hesperia;
and now, at the urging of wise Carmentis, he had steered his craft into the river
and was going upstream against the Tuscan waters:
she looks at the river's bank, where the shallows of Tarentum lie,
and at the huts scattered through the lonely places;
and just as she was, with her hair streaming, she stood before the stern
and fiercely held back the hand of the one steering the course,
and stretching her arms far out towards the right bank
she struck the pine deck three times with frenzied foot;
and, so that she would not leap ashore in her haste to stand on land,
she was barely, barely held back by Evander's hand.
“Hail, gods of the places we have sought,” she said,
“and you, land that will give new gods to heaven,
and rivers and springs that this hospitable land enjoys,
and nymphs of the groves and bands of Naiads!
May you appear with good omens to my son and me,
and may this bank be touched by a lucky foot!
Am I mistaken, or will these hills become mighty walls,
and will the rest of the earth seek its laws from this land?
To these hills one day the whole world is promised:
who would believe the place holds so great a destiny?
Soon Dardanian pines will touch these shores:
here too a woman will be the cause of a new war.
Dear grandson, Pallas, why do you put on deadly armour?
Put it on! You will not be slain with a lowly avenger.
Conquered, Troy, you will yet conquer, and overthrown, you will rise again:
that ruin of yours will bury the houses of your enemies.
Burn Neptune's Pergamum, victorious flames!
Is this ash not, even so, higher than the whole world?
Soon dutiful Aeneas the sacred objects and, a second sacred charge, his father
will bring here: receive, Vesta, the gods of Ilium!
A time will come when the same one will guard both you and the world,
and the rites will be performed with a god himself tending them,
and the guardianship of the fatherland will remain with the Augusti:
it is right that this house should hold the reins of empire.
From it the grandson and son of a god, though he himself refuses,
will bear his father's burdens with a heavenly mind;
and as I shall one day be consecrated on everlasting altars,
so Julia Augusta will be a new divinity.”
When with such words she had come down to our own years,
her prophetic tongue stopped in mid-speech.
There was no long delay: the new dwellings stood, and no one
on the Ausonian hills was greater than the Arcadian.
Look, the hero brings the cattle of Erytheia there,
the club-bearer, having travelled the long road across the world;
and while the house of Tegea gives him lodging, the cattle wander
unguarded through the broad fields.
It was morning: shaken from sleep, the Tirynthian herdsman
notices that two bulls are missing from the count.
Searching, he sees no tracks of the silent theft:
fierce Cacus had dragged them backwards into his cave,
Cacus, the terror and the disgrace of the Aventine wood,
no small evil to neighbours and strangers.
The man had a dreadful face, strength to match his body, and his body
was huge: the father of this monster was Mulciber;
and for a house [he had] a huge cave with long recesses,
hidden away, hardly to be found even by the wild beasts themselves;
over the doorposts hang heads and nailed-up arms,
and the filthy ground is white with human bones.
The son of Jupiter was leaving, with part of his cattle ill kept:
the stolen ones gave out a lowing with a hoarse sound.
‘I accept the call back,’ he says, and, following the voice,
he came as avenger through the woods to the impious cave.
Cacus had blocked the entrance with a barrier of broken-off mountain;
twice five yoke [of oxen] could scarcely have moved that mass.
Here he strains with his shoulders (the sky too had rested on them)
and by his heaving loosens the huge weight.
As soon as it was overturned, the crash terrified the upper air itself,
and the ground, struck by the weight of the mass, sank down.
Cacus first begins the fight hand to hand
and fiercely wages it with rocks and logs.
When these achieve nothing, he flees, his courage failing, to his father's arts
and vomits flames from his roaring mouth;
whenever he breathes them out, you would think Typhoeus was breathing
and a swift lightning bolt was hurled from Etna's fire.
Alcides strikes first, and the three-knotted club, swung back,
lands three, four times full in the man's face.
He falls, and vomits smoke mixed with blood,
and, dying, beats the ground with his broad chest.
One bull from among them he sacrifices to you, Jupiter,
as victor, and calls Evander and the country folk,
and sets up for himself the altar that is called the Greatest,
here, where a part of the city takes its name from the ox.
Nor is Evander's mother silent that the time is near
when the earth will have had enough use of its Hercules.
He spoke, and as lasting memorials of the ancient deed
the Snake, the Bird and the Bowl shine as neighbouring stars.
The third dawn after the Ides sees the naked Luperci,
and the rites of two-horned Faunus go forward.
Tell, Pierian Muses, what the origin of the rites is,
and from where they were brought when they reached Latin homes.
Pan, the god of the flock, is said to have been worshipped of old by the
Arcadians: he abounds on the Arcadian ridges.
Pholoe will be witness, witness the waters of Stymphalus,
and the Ladon, which runs to the sea with swift waters,
and the ridges of the Nonacrian grove, ringed with pinewoods,
and high Cyllene, and the Parrhasian snows.
Pan was the god of the herd there, Pan the deity of the mares;
he received gifts for keeping the sheep safe.
Evander brought the woodland deities over with him;
here, where the city is now, there was then the site of a city.
So we worship the god, and the rites brought by the Pelasgians
the *flamen Dialis* [priest of Jupiter] still performs in the ancient manner.
Why then do they run, and why (for such is the custom of running)
do they bare their bodies, setting aside their clothes, you ask?
The swift god himself loves to run about on the high
mountains, and himself breaks into sudden flight;
the god himself is naked and bids his ministers go naked,
and clothing was not convenient enough for running.
Before Jupiter was born, they say, the land was held by the
Arcadians, and that people was older than the moon.
Their life was like that of beasts, spent in no useful pursuits:
the common folk were still rough and without skill.
The story of the deed remains: they run with their clothing laid aside,
and, since it turned out well, it keeps a remembering fame.
Perhaps you may also ask why that place is [called] the Lupercal,
or what reason marks the day with such a name.
Silvia the Vestal had borne heavenly offspring
while her uncle held the kingdom.
He orders the little ones to be taken away and killed in the river:
What are you doing? One of these will be Romulus.
Protesting, the servants carry out the tearful orders;
yet they weep, and carry the twins to the place ordered.
The Albula, which Tiberinus, drowned in its waters, turned into the Tiber,
happened to be swollen with winter waters:
here, where the forums now are, you could have seen boats wandering,
and where your valleys lie, Circus Maximus.
When they came here (for they could not go on
any further), one and then another of them says:
‘But how alike they are! And how beautiful each one is!
Yet of the two, this one has more vigour.
If lineage is shown by the face, unless appearance deceives,
I suspect that some god or other is in you—
but if any god were the author of your origin,
in so desperate a moment
he would bring help; your mother would surely bring help, if she were not herself in need of help,
she who was made a mother and bereaved on one day.
Born together, about to die together, together go beneath the waves,
bodies!’ He had finished, and set them down from his bosom.
Both wailed together: you would think they had understood.
The men go back to their homes with wet cheeks.
The hollow trough holds them up, set in it, on the surface of the water:
ah, how much destiny a little plank carried!
The trough, driven into the mud by the shady woods,
settles little by little as the river falls.
There was a tree: traces remain; and what is now called
the Rumina fig was the Romula fig.
To the abandoned twins came (a marvel!) a she-wolf that had just whelped:
who would believe that the wild beast did not harm the boys?
Not harming is too little: she even helps them. Those a she-wolf nurses
kindred hands brought themselves to destroy.
She stood still and fawns with her tail on her tender nurslings
and shapes their two bodies with her tongue.
You would know they were sons of Mars: fear was absent; they draw at the udders
and are nourished by the help of milk not promised to them.
She gave the place its name, and the place gave it to the Luperci.
The nurse has a great reward for the milk she gave.
What forbids [us to think] the Luperci were named from the Arcadian mountain?
Faunus Lycaeus has temples in Arcadia.
Bride, what are you waiting for? Not by potent herbs
nor by prayer nor magic spell will you become a mother;
accept with patience the blows of the fertilising right hand;
soon your father-in-law will have the longed-for name of grandfather.
For there was a day when, by a harsh lot, wives
were rendering few pledges of their wombs.
Hence they think it wrong to put this kind [of creature] on their tables,
and the timid Syrians do not defile their mouths with fish.
The next day is free, but the third is assigned to Quirinus;
he who holds this name was formerly Romulus,
either because the ancient Sabines called a spear *curis*
(the warlike god came to the stars named from his weapon),
or because the Quirites gave their own name to their king,
or because he had joined Cures to the Romans.
For the father mighty in arms, after he had seen the new walls
and many wars brought to an end by Romulus' hand,
said: “Jupiter, Roman power has strength:
it does not need the service of my blood.
Give back the son to his father; although the other has perished,
the one who remains to me will count for himself and for Remus.
‘There will be one whom you shall raise to the blue of heaven’:
you said this to me; let Jupiter's words be made good.”
Jupiter nodded. At his nod both
poles shook, and Atlas shifted the weight of the sky.
There is a place the ancients called the Goat's Marsh:
there by chance, Romulus, you were giving judgments to your people;
the sun fled, and rising clouds blotted out the sky,
and a heavy rainstorm fell in streaming waters.
Here it thunders, there the sky is split by hurled fires:
people flee; the king was making for the stars with his father's horses.
There was mourning, and the senators were falsely accused of murder,
and that belief might perhaps have stuck in people's minds;
but Proculus Julius was coming from Alba Longa,
and the moon was shining, and there was no need of a torch,
when suddenly the hedges on his left shook and moved:
he stepped back, and his hair stood on end.
Handsome, larger than human, and splendid in a robe of state,
Romulus seemed to stand in the middle of the road
and at the same time to say: “Forbid the Quirites to mourn,
and let them not profane my divinity with their tears;
let the dutiful crowd bring incense and appease the new Quirinus,
and let them cultivate their fathers' arts and warfare.” He gave the command,
and vanished from his eyes into thin air;
he calls the people together and reports the words as commanded.
Temples are built for the god, the hill too is named after him,
and fixed days bring round the ancestral rites.
Why the same day is also called the Feast of Fools,
hear: the reason is small, but a fitting one lies behind it.
They named this day Feralia, because they bring the dues [to the dead];
that day is the last for appeasing the shades.
Look, an aged old woman, sitting among the girls,
performs rites to Tacita (and yet she herself is not silent),
and with three fingers places three [lumps of] incense under the threshold,
where the little mouse has made itself a hidden path;
then she binds enchanted threads with dark lead
and turns seven black beans over in her mouth,
and what she has sealed with pitch and pierced with a bronze needle,
the sewn-up head of a sprat, she roasts in the fire;
she drips in wine as well: whatever wine is left over
either she or her companions drink, but she drinks more.
‘We have bound hostile tongues and unfriendly mouths,’
she says as she leaves, and the old woman goes out drunk.
At once you will ask me who the goddess Muta is:
learn what I know from old men of long ago.
Jupiter, overcome by immoderate love for Juturna,
As soon as she reached the pools of her sister Juturna,
“Flee the banks,” she said, and repeated Jupiter's words.
She also went to Juno, and, pitying wives,
said: “Your husband loves the Naiad Juturna.”
Jupiter swelled with anger, and the tongue she had used without restraint
he tears out of her, and calls Mercury:
He prepares to use force; she pleads with her face instead of words,
and strives in vain to speak with her mute mouth.
She becomes pregnant and bears twins, who guard the crossroads
and keep watch in our city always: the Lares.
Dear kinsfolk named the next day the Caristia,
and the crowd of relatives comes to the family gods.
nor would Othryades have been read on the heaped-up arms;
oh, how much blood he gave for his country!
What of when the new Capitol was being built? Of course, of the gods,
the whole crowd yielded to Jupiter and gave up their place:
Terminus, as the ancients relate, was found in the shrine,
stayed where he was, and shares the temple with great Jupiter.
Even now, so that he may see nothing above him but the stars,
the temple roof has a small opening.
You were unarmed then too, when the Roman priestess
captivated you, so that you might give great seed to this city.
Silvia the Vestal (for what forbids me to begin from there?)
was going in the morning to fetch water to wash the sacred things;
she had come to the bank that slopes down by a gentle path:
the earthenware urn is set down from the top of her head.
Tired, she sat down on the ground and let the breezes play on her open
breast, and put her ruffled hair back in order.
While she sits, the shady willows and the singing birds
brought on sleep, and the light murmur of the water.
Sweet rest stole secretly over her overcome eyes,
and her hand, gone limp, falls from her chin.
Mars sees her, desires her when seen, and takes her when desired,
and by his divine power his stolen love went unnoticed.
Sleep leaves her; she lies heavy: already, of course, within
her womb was the founder of the Roman city.
Languid she rises, and does not know why she rises languid,
and leaning against a tree she utters these words:
“May it be helpful and lucky, I pray, what in the semblance of sleep
I saw; or was it clearer than a dream?
I was at the fires of Ilium, when, slipping from my hair,
the woollen headband fell down before the sacred hearth;
from it two palms together, wonderful to see,
sprang up: of them, one was the greater,
and with its heavy branches had covered the whole world
and had touched the stars with its topmost foliage.
Then see, my uncle wields an axe against them:
I am terrified at the warning, and my heart throbs with fear.
The woodpecker, bird of Mars, fights for the twin trunks,
and the she-wolf: through them both palms were safe.”
She spoke, and the full urn, with strength not steady,
she lifted; she had filled it while telling her vision.
Meanwhile, as Remus grew, as Quirinus grew,
her belly was swelling with its heavenly burden.
Short of the year's ending, with its courses run,
two signs now remained for the shining god:
Silvia becomes a mother. Vesta's images are said
to have put their virgin hands before their eyes;
the goddess's altar certainly trembled as her servant gave birth,
and the frightened flame sank beneath its ashes.
When Amulius, scorner of justice, learned this
(for, as victor, he held the power seized from his brother),
When they heard of their lineage, the revelation of their father raises their spirits,
and they are ashamed to have a name among a few huts.
And Amulius falls, run through by Romulus' sword,
and the kingdom is restored to their aged grandfather.
Walls are founded, which, though they were small,
it still did not profit Remus to have leapt over.
Who will tell me now why the Salii carry the heavenly
arms of Mars and sing of Mamurius?
Nymph, tell me, you who serve Diana's grove and lake;
nymph, wife of Numa, come to your own deeds.
In the valley of Aricia, ringed by a dark wood,
there is a lake, sacred with ancient religion.
Here Hippolytus lies hidden, torn apart by his horses' reins,
and so no horses enter that grove.
Threads hang down, veiling the long hedges,
and many a tablet has been set up to the deserving goddess.
A stony brook flows down with a fitful murmur:
I have often drunk from it, but in small draughts.
It is Egeria who supplies the water, a goddess dear to the Camenae;
she was Numa's wife and counsellor.
At first it was decided that the Quirites, too quick to go to war,
should be softened by law and the fear of the gods;
and a man who was savage a moment ago is changed at the sight of an altar
and offers wine and salted spelt on the warm hearths.
Look, the father of the gods scatters red flames through the clouds
and drains the sky by pouring out its waters;
never at any other time did the hurled fires fall more thickly:
the king is afraid, and terror grips the hearts of the common people.
To him the goddess [said]: ‘Do not be too afraid! The thunderbolt
can be expiated,’ she says, ‘and the anger of savage Jupiter is turned aside.
But the rite of expiation Picus and Faunus will be able
to hand on, both of them divinities of Roman soil.
Nor will they hand it on without force: put chains on them once they are caught.’
And so she revealed by what art they could be caught.
Beneath the Aventine lay a grove, dark with the shade of holm-oak,
at the sight of which you could say: ‘There is a divinity here.’
In the middle [was] grass, and, covered with green moss,
a never-failing stream of water trickled from a rock:
from it, as a rule, Faunus and Picus alone used to drink.
Here King Numa comes and sacrifices a sheep to the spring,
and sets out cups full of fragrant wine,
and, hidden in a cave with his men, he himself lies concealed.
The woodland divinities come to their accustomed springs
and refresh their dry breasts with plenty of unmixed wine.
Sleep follows the wine; Numa comes out of the cold cave
and puts the sleepers' hands into tight bonds.
When sleep had gone, they try by struggling to break
the bonds: the more they struggle, the tighter the bonds hold.
Then Numa: ‘Gods of the groves, forgive what I have done,
if you know that wickedness is far from my nature;
and show [me] in what way the thunderbolt can be expiated.’
So Numa; so Faunus speaks, shaking his horns:
‘You ask for great things, and things not lawful for you to learn
through our telling: our divine powers have their limits.
We are gods of the countryside, who hold sway on the high
mountains: Jupiter has the say over his own weapons.
Him you will not be able to draw down from the sky by yourself,
but perhaps you will be able to, if you use our help.’
Faunus had said this; Picus' view is the same:
‘But take the chains off us,’ Picus says:
